title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: a poor boy who wanted milk becomes the sage who hands Krishna the names, and the names are gathered up as Mahadeva

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave us Kapardin, the braided-haired wild god a Vedic poet asked to keep a village well. What small thing did you do for the place you live? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

A little boy wants milk. He's seen another child drink it, and he goes to his mother and asks. They're poor, living in a forest hermitage, and there's no milk to give. So she stirs some flour into water and hands it to him. He drinks it, and knows it isn't milk. That small kitchen moment is where the Mahabharata begins the story of Upamanyu, the sage we met at the start of this run, the one who handed Krishna Shiva's names. Today, the last selection from the Shiva Sahasranama goes back to where the names came from.
screen: `A BOY ASKS FOR MILK.` → `FLOUR IN WATER.` → `WHERE THE NAMES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, Upamanyu tells Krishna his own story. When the boy cries over the flour and water, his mother tells him they have nothing, and that only Shiva can give what he's asking for. So the boy sets out to worship Shiva, and he does it with his whole small life, in hard austerities. One day a visitor arrives: Indra, king of the gods, riding his white elephant, offering the boy any gift he wants. Upamanyu turns him down. He wants nothing that doesn't come from Shiva. And then the visitor changes. It was Shiva all along, testing him, and now Shiva shows himself, with Parvati beside him, and gives the boy far more than milk. That's who Krishna is sitting with when he hears the names: someone who asked for one thing and was given the god himself. When Upamanyu has taught him, Krishna worships Shiva, and Shiva and Parvati appear to him too, and grant his wish for a son. Across this run of selections we've gathered a handful of the names. Sthanu, the post. Shankara and Shambhu, the makers of well-being. Pashupati, who loosens the rope. Nilakantha, the blue throat. Kapardin, the wild one a village asks for help. And Vishnu's lotuses, an offering at every name. One more name gathers them up: Mahadeva, the great god. Not great like a king who keeps his distance. Great like the one who turned up at a poor boy's hermitage, and answered him. The list is long because the god is large. But the story at its root is small: a child, a cup, an honest no to everything else.
screen: `UPAMANYU REFUSES INDRA'S GIFTS.` · `SHIVA REVEALS HIMSELF.` · `KRISHNA RECEIVES HIS WISH.` · `MAHADEVA GATHERS THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk back through the names you've met. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then, one per breath, let each name pass through your mind like a bead on a string. Sthanu, steady. Shankara, well-being. Pashupati, the loosened rope. Nilakantha, the held poison. Kapardin, the village kept well. Mahadeva. Notice which one you linger on. That's the one that's yours for now. If you pray, you can say that name a few times, slowly. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. The hymn of Shiva's names, taught by Upamanyu, the boy who wanted milk, and gathered up today as Mahadeva, the great god.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, keep the one name you lingered on, and bring it to mind once when you're waiting for something. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva address him as Mahadeva in daily speech and worship, and some recite his sahasranama in full on Mondays or on Maha Shivaratri, offering something at each name.

fork.setup: you're a boy who has worshipped Shiva for a long time. Indra, king of the gods, arrives and offers you any gift you want. what do you say?
options: take the gift: Indra is a great god too.
say no: you want nothing that isn't from Shiva.
fork.reveal: Upamanyu says no. the visitor turns out to be Shiva, testing him, and Shiva shows himself.

original.note: Sanskrit: Mahadeva, the great (maha) god (deva); a name of Shiva.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mahadeva just means Shiva is the biggest god.
what it means: the great god who came to a poor boy's hermitage, a name that gathers up all the others.
what a scholar hears: the Anushasana Parva's frame, Upamanyu's boyhood and Indra's test, around the names he teaches Krishna.

notes: Selection seven of seven; tomorrow begins Kashmir Shaivism (the Shiva Sutras). Paraphrased from the Anushasana Parva: Upamanyu as a boy asking for milk, his mother giving flour mixed in water, telling him only Shiva can give it, his austerities, Shiva coming in Indra's form on the white elephant, Upamanyu refusing, Shiva revealing himself with Parvati. Krishna's worship and Shiva and Parvati granting him a son (Samba). Confirm details and the order in which the epic tells them.
The text gives a length for Upamanyu's austerities; it is left out here to avoid a count.
